read.title: Following the airway
text: Air entering the body passes a series of structures, and each has its own root. It enters through the nose (rhin/o or nas/o) and moves through the pharynx (pharyng/o), the throat passage shared with food. It then passes the larynx (laryng/o), the voice box, guarded by the epiglottis, a flap that closes over the airway during swallowing. The trachea (trache/o) carries air into the chest, where it splits into two bronchi (bronch/o) and then into smaller and smaller branches.

The branches end in millions of alveoli, tiny air sacs where oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out. The lungs themselves have three roots, pneum/o, pneumon/o and pulmon/o, and are wrapped in the pleura. Below them sits the diaphragm, named phren/o.

Breathing words are built on -pnea. Apnea is the absence of breathing, dyspnea is difficult breathing, tachypnea is rapid breathing and eupnea is normal breathing. Gases have roots too: ox/i for oxygen and capn/o for carbon dioxide, so hypoxia is too little oxygen in the tissues and hypercapnia is too much carbon dioxide in the blood.
